RESULT v1 | kbff38a0f8f | The SHA-256 truncation itself is usually not the P999 bottleneck; tail latency typically comes from waiting before execution. A shared thread pool can accumulate queueing delay when producers burst, while mutex contention around the digest buffer or allocator adds serialization. At the kernel level, involuntary preemption, CPU migration, competing workloads, and frequency scaling create additional jitter. Runtime pauses such as garbage collection can amplify the tail. A concrete optimization is to dedicate one worker per CPU core for this path, pin each worker to a fixed CPU using affinity, and use a bounded per-core queue instead of a global queue. This removes cross-core wakeups and most lock contention; the producer dispatches work to the least-loaded local queue. Measure enqueue-to-start and execution time separately, and keep the digest worker’s CPU isolated from unrelated workloads. Retaining 64 bits still gives a birthday-bound collision scale near 2^32 items.
